title: Other views of the table
hook: Lutherans: Christ truly present in, with and under; Calvin: spiritual feeding; Zwingli: memorial

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Real Presence: transubstantiation, the Catholic word for bread and wine becoming Christ's body and blood, and the Orthodox, who call the change a mystery. Your line was a holy mystery. What did you bow to? Day one thousand one hundred two.

One table, one loaf, and a long argument about it. Paul says it happened on the night Jesus was betrayed. In Luke's telling, Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, hands it round, and adds a request: "this do in remembrance of me." Churches still keep that request. Yesterday we heard how Catholics and the Orthodox read his other words at that table, "Take, eat; this is my body." Today, the same table seen from three more chairs, each taking hold of one small word in that sentence a different way. Is. Today's word: other views of the table.

Start with Martin Luther, who held on hard to that little word. Lutherans teach that Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine. The bread stays bread, and Christ is really there, given into your hand. Lutherans don't try to explain how; they take the words as spoken. Then John Calvin, in Geneva. Calvin taught that believers truly feed on Christ, but by the Holy Spirit, who lifts them up to him, rather than by Christ's body coming down into the bread. Real food, received by faith. Reformed and Presbyterian churches stand in that line. Then Huldrych Zwingli, in Zurich. Zwingli read is as signifies, the way someone points at a photo and says, that's my grandmother. For him the meal is a memorial: the church remembers, gives thanks, and is joined together as one body. Baptist churches, among others, speak of the meal as an ordinance: something Jesus commanded, done in remembrance. But remembering, in Paul, is more than thinking back. When he passes the words on to Corinth, he adds: "For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come." Remembering is something the church does, out loud, together. And when Paul scolds Corinth about the supper, the first trouble he names isn't theory. It's how they treat each other: some go hungry while others eat first. His fix is plain: "when ye come together to eat, tarry one for another." Wait for each other. Lutheran, Reformed and memorial churches read the meal differently, and say so honestly. None of their views lets anyone skip that verse.

Here's the practice: share bread thoughtfully. If there's bread nearby, or a cracker, or anything to eat, take it, and before you eat, stop. Breathe slowly. Notice that it came through many hands: a field, a baker, a truck, a shelf, someone who set it out. If someone is with you, offer them some first, and wait until they have it. If you're alone, bring to mind one person you'd want at your table. If you pray, you can give thanks before you eat, in words you already know. If you don't, let the pause itself be the thanks. The bell holds the time.
Other views of the table. Lutherans: Christ present in, with and under the bread. Calvin: feeding on Christ by the Spirit. Zwingli: a meal of remembrance.

segments.voice: Your line: do this in memory. Today, at one meal, wait until everyone has food before you begin. Small, and as old as Corinth. Day one thousand one hundred two.

howItsDone: Lutheran, Reformed, Presbyterian, Baptist and other Protestant churches all keep the Lord's Supper, under names like communion or the Lord's Supper, and they explain Christ's presence in it in different ways.
